name: Rafael Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential. Shall we start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm not very exciting, I should say. I translate manuals.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Manuals are fine. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate German into English, mostly technical documents: maintenance manuals for wind turbines, safety sheets for pumps, that kind of thing. Most of it comes through two agencies, and one wind turbine maker sends me work directly. I work from the spare desk in the flat I co-own with my brother, and on Thursdays I cycle to a co-working space so I talk to actual humans. A good day is six thousand words; a bad day is two thousand and a lot of searching for what a 'Blattlagerschmierung' is in English.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Blade bearing lubrication, it turns out. That's the job, really: knowing the machine well enough that the words make sense. I'm still slow at it, because I only have a languages degree, not engineering. The senior translators I know can do twice my speed because they've seen every turbine part ten times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. That's more or less the world I already work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. The tools are handy for checking terminology, but nobody should trust a machine with a safety sheet. I'd say that in the freelancers' association forum, where everyone already argues about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still matters to me, because my agencies already use 'fuzzy match' discounts. That means they pay me less for any sentence that looks like one translated before, and with manuals that's a lot of sentences. My rate per word has dropped about ten percent in two years, and a plateau doesn't undo that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as I do now, and keep using the AI glossary checker the agency gave us when I'm unsure of a term. I'd join the freelancers' association properly, not just read the forum, because they're pushing for minimum rates. And I'd keep putting a few hundred a month aside, because that habit costs me nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy. The flat is half mine, I have about ten months saved, and there are plenty of agencies in this city. It's more the slow drip of lower rates that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is a few hundred a month, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 350. My brother Jonas pays half the mortgage, and the lodger in the third bedroom covers the bills, so my costs are low. Splitting a flat with my brother is the only reason a junior translator like me has savings at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the association pushes for minimum rates. What would that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing quickly. But the agencies set the rates alone right now, and freelancers like me just accept them. I'd like there to be someone on the other side of the table.

do: **Keep translating** manuals and use the agency's glossary checker when unsure.
Join the **freelancers' association** properly, not just read the forum.

steps.text: Keep translating turbine manuals for the same three clients
Use the agency glossary checker on tricky terms
Join the freelancers' association and its minimum-rate push

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is actually happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say post-editing should be paid properly, not at half rate, and that machines checking machines is how a turbine ends up with the wrong bolt torque. I'd say we need standards for who signs off a safety document. That's my public line, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, manuals are exactly what AI does well: repetitive, structured, the same parts again and again. The agencies would send me machine drafts to fix instead of real translation. I think my income drops maybe thirty percent within two years, and I'm the junior one, so I'm also the one they'd stop calling first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a proper post-editing course this winter, the one the association runs for about 400, so I stop being slow at it. I'd ask the turbine maker if I can be the person who checks and signs off their safety documents. And I'd push the association's campaign for a minimum post-editing rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. I can see the shape of it. I just don't like that I'm the one most likely to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I might need him to cover more of the mortgage for a few months, and he'd say fine, because I covered him when he changed jobs. We'd sit on the balcony and go through the numbers. My brother Jonas is an electrician, so he'd also tell me to come and learn a real trade, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign off safety documents. Why would they pay a junior for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. They might not. But somebody has to put their name on the English version, and I'd rather be learning that job than fixing commas for an agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then my job is gone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to tax these companies and pay people a basic income while they retrain. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it everywhere, including at the association. It's not radical when it's happening to everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in 2028 nobody pays me to translate a manual, full stop. Maybe a year longer for sign-off, until regulators catch up. But the robots coming about three years later matters to me, because the hands-on work in a wind farm would still need people until roughly 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away for the wind turbine technician apprenticeship that my direct client runs, because they already know me and I know their manuals in two languages. I'd stop spending on anything big and keep my ten months of savings for the training year. And I'd raise the lodger's rent a little, which feels bad, but it's below market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just saying 2028. But having the apprenticeship idea helps, because at least I know where I'd go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Climbing turbines is a long way from a desk. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. I'm scared of heights, honestly. But I've translated the climbing safety manual three times, so I know exactly how they keep people alive up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd have three years of good pay and savings, and maybe a supervisor role checking the robots. Beyond that I'd be guessing, and I don't like guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a more sensible amount of panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about taxing the companies and supporting retraining, but I'd also say: start now, don't wait for 2031. I'd want the association to run courses, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to learn the turbines properly without jumping off a cliff. I'd still translate for two or three years, which pays the bills. Then by 2031 the translation stops, and the hands-on work runs until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the turbine maker this year about a junior field-service role that mixes documents and site work, so I'd keep a foot in both. I'd do an evening electrical course, about two years, the one Jonas did. And I'd keep translating while I can, and save harder, maybe 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I can believe in. It's less of a jump and more of a staircase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the freelance work while you're doing evening classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shrinks. I'd drop the worse-paying agency and keep the direct client. That's maybe a fifth less income, but I can carry that for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said start now. What would you tell another junior translator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't spend five years getting faster at something that ends in 2031. Learn the thing next to your work, the thing your clients actually build or do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that one I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, and we should use it for public training money and proper protections for freelancers. I'd say it in the association and probably write something for its newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the next few years look a lot like today for me. I'd translate, get better, save, and around 2031 start moving into technical work. I'm young enough that changing at thirty-two isn't a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and use the AI tools a bit more as they prove themselves, so I'm faster and earn more. I'd put money into a pension and a savings account each month. And around year four or five I'd take the electrical course and talk to the turbine maker about site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Lots of people change careers once. I'd just know my date in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd not do with ten years that you would with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't climb turbines yet, which my mother would be glad about. I'd also stay in translation long enough to actually get good at it, which I'd like for my own pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older translators who are fifty-five in 2036 and too young to retire. I'd worry about them more than me, and I'd want the association to fight for them first.

Freelancers need **proper protections** before the change arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be changing careers while scared of heights, with no time to do it slowly. What would help is a paid apprenticeship scheme for adults, so I'm not living on savings for the training year. A basic income during retraining would help even more, but I'm not holding my breath.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who checks the robots' manuals. Every machine needs instructions in twenty languages, and someone will have to be responsible when they're wrong. I'd like that someone to be a person with a name.

headlineQuote: Every machine needs instructions in twenty languages, and someone will have to be responsible when they're wrong.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **German-English** translator of wind turbine and pump manuals.
He co-owns a flat with his brother, which gives him **low costs** and real savings.
He adopts **AI tools** once they're proven and backs the freelancers' association.
Across the scenarios he plans a move from manuals to **hands-on turbine work**, using the robot delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing a career change at speed while scared of heights.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** scheme so the training year isn't funded by savings.
A **basic income** during retraining, though he doubts it will come.
